questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman with known Addison's disease presents with vomiting and diarrhoea for 24 hours. BP 84/52, HR 118. She has taken no oral hydrocortisone today because she cannot keep it down.
options: Double her usual oral hydrocortisone dose
IM/IV hydrocortisone 100mg and IV fluid resuscitation
Oral rehydration and review in 24 hours
questions.explanation: This is an adrenal crisis. She cannot absorb oral steroid, so the sick-day rule of doubling the oral dose no longer applies — the answer is parenteral hydrocortisone 100mg plus aggressive IV saline. Fludrocortisone has no role acutely: at stress doses hydrocortisone provides ample mineralocorticoid activity.

questions.stem: A 51-year-old man is being investigated for fatigue and postural dizziness. Short Synacthen test: baseline cortisol 140 nmol/L, 30-minute cortisol 260 nmol/L (pass threshold ~430–450). ACTH is markedly elevated.
options: No adrenal insufficiency; investigate other causes
questions.explanation: The Synacthen test fails (260 is well below threshold), so adrenal insufficiency is confirmed. ACTH markedly elevated means the pituitary is driving hard and the adrenal is not responding — the defect is at the gland: primary. In secondary and tertiary disease ACTH is low or inappropriately normal, because the problem is upstream. ACTH high → primary; ACTH low → secondary.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman on warfarin for atrial fibrillation has an INR of 6.2. She has no bleeding and is otherwise well.
questions.lead: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Withhold warfarin and give oral vitamin K
Continue warfarin unchanged and recheck in a week
questions.explanation: Raised INR without bleeding is managed by withholding warfarin ± low-dose oral vitamin K, then rechecking. Prothrombinex and IV vitamin K are reserved for major or life-threatening bleeding — using them here over-corrects and risks thrombosis in a patient anticoagulated for a reason. Matching intensity of reversal to severity of bleeding is the point being tested.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man on dabigatran for AF is admitted with melaena and haemodynamic instability.
questions.explanation: Idarucizumab is the specific monoclonal antibody reversal agent for dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor. Andexanet alfa reverses the factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban). Protamine reverses heparin; vitamin K reverses warfarin. Matching agent to drug class is the discriminator — dabigatran is also dialysable, unlike the Xa inhibitors.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with small cell lung cancer develops proximal weakness, oedema and new hypertension over 6 weeks. He is not cushingoid in appearance.
questions.lead: Which biochemical pattern fits ectopic ACTH secretion?
questions.explanation: Ectopic ACTH causes cortisol excess, and very high cortisol saturates 11β-HSD2 so it acts on mineralocorticoid receptors: hypokalaemia, metabolic alkalosis, hyperglycaemia. The rapid onset means classic Cushingoid habitus has not developed — weakness, oedema and hypertension dominate instead. Option 1 is the pattern of cortisol deficiency, the exact inversion worth being able to recite in both directions.
